newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian Alan Bond jailed for fraud, again.
newsitem.headline: Australian Alan Bond jailed for fraud, again.

text.p: Failed Australian entrepreneur Alan Bond was sentenced Wednesday to four years in prison for his role in the biggest corporate fraud in Australian history worth A$1.0 billion ($766 million).
But Bond could be released on parole in 1998 after serving a minimum one-year non-parole period.
Bond, 58, already serving a three-year sentence for an earlier fraud, pleaded guilty to two charges of dishonesty last December.
Judge Michael Murray said the latest sentence was to be served concurrently with his present sentence, under which he would have been released in August 1997.
After serving the one-year minimum non-parole period of his latest sentence, Bond would be eligible for release in 1998.
The prosecutor had asked the judge to jail Bond for a maximum 10 years.

In sentencing Bond, Murray said mitigating circumstances included Bond's age, his substantial contribution to the community, his offer to co-operate in other cases, the stain and humiliation of conviction and his early pleas of guilty.
"To some degree (the pleas) expressed the settled view of the strength of the prosecution case but there was also an element of significant remorse," Murray said.
"You did not immediately express that remorse but there was evidence of a growing acceptance of your wrongdoing and a willingness to take responsibility for it," he said.

Bond admitted that in 1988 and 1989 he failed to act honestly as a company director and acted with intent to defraud when he created a A$1.0 billion unsecured loan from Bell Resources to his ailing Bond Corp.
"Over the years which followed Bell Resources Ltd was able to recover some money but it is estimated that its losses amounted to many hundreds of millions of dollars," Murray said.
Bond pleaded guilty after the prosecution agreed to drop another five charges relating to the Bell Resources fraud, which followed Bond Corp. taking control of the Bell Group Ltd in mid-1988.
Bond was jailed for three years in August for fraud involving the French impressionist painting, La Promenade.

He was also jailed for 2-1/2 years in 1992 after being found guilty of inducing a former friend to contribute to the rescue of a Western Australia bank while concealing a A$16 million ($12.3 million) fee for his own company.
He served only a few months in jail before a second jury acquitted him at a retrial.
Bond was named Australian of the Year after winning the America's Cup yacht race in 1983.

His personal fortune was estimated at A$350 million ($268 million) in the late 1980s before the collapse of his brewing, mining and property empire, Bond Corporation Holdings Ltd, under debt totalling A$600 million ($459.8 million).

Bond, a former sign painter who built a global network of companies with interests spanning mining, property, media and breweries, was declared bankrupt in April 1995, but was freed of bankruptcy in February 1996.
